## Why This Is Asked

This probes practical enforcement of identity-bound service access in a multi-tenant cluster, combining service mesh, policy-as-code, and runtime validation.

## Key Concepts

- SPIFFE IDs and mTLS
- Istio AuthorizationPolicy
- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate/Constraint
- Tenant isolation and RBAC

## Code Example

```yaml
# Istio AuthorizationPolicy (compliant example)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: mongodb-per-tenant-access
  namespace: tenantA
spec:
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["spiffe://cluster/tenantA/pod-1"]
    to:
    - operation:
        ports: ["27017"]
```

```yaml
# Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate (pseudo)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sspiffe
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: SPIFFEIsTenantScoped
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8sspiffe
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        input.review.kind.kind == "Pod"
        not input.review.object.metadata.annotations["spiffe-id"]
        msg := "Pod must have a tenant-scoped SPIFFE ID annotation"
      }
```

- How would you test cross-tenant data access failures?
- How would you monitor and alert on violations and drift?

```rego
package terraform.enforcement

default allow = false

violation[{"msg": m}] {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "snowflake_share"
  rc.change.actions contains "create"
  not rc.change.after.tags.approved == true

}

violation[{"msg": m}] {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "aws_s3_bucket"
  rc.change.actions contains "create"

}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests understanding of basic CI gates for Kubernetes manifests and how to enforce namespace discipline across a multi-service repository. It demonstrates practical knowledge of YAML parsing, GitHub Actions, and Kubernetes resource management.

## Key Concepts

- **YAML manifest parsing with yq**: Using yq to extract and validate metadata.namespace fields across all Kubernetes manifests
- **Namespace discipline**: Enforcing non-default namespaces prevents accidental deployments to unintended environments and ensures proper resource isolation
- **Lightweight CI gates**: Simple, fast validation scripts every PR without that run on requiring external tools or complex infrastructure
- **Cluster-scoped vs namespace-scoped resources**: Understanding when to omit namespace (ClusterRole, CRDs) versus when it must be present (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap)

## What Separates Good Answers from Great Ones

A great answer recognizes that not all Kubernetes resources are namespace-scoped. Cluster-scoped resources like ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding, CustomResourceDefinition, and Nodes must be excluded from this validation. The candidate should handle this edge case gracefully, either by skipping these resource types or by documenting the assumption that only namespace-scoped resources are being validated.

## Why This Is Asked

Real-world cross-cloud serverless platforms demand automated image signing and artifact attestations. This question tests end-to-end workflow design, policy enforcement decisions, and practical CI/CD integration skills.

## Key Concepts

- Cosign signing and verification
- Rekor attestations for transparency and auditability
- SBOM generation (using tools like Syft)
- Multi-cloud serverless deployment patterns
- GitHub Actions workflow integration

## Code Example

```yaml
name: cks-serverless-sign
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Install cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3

      - name: Set up Syft for SBOM
        uses: anchore/syft-action@v1

      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/serverless-fn:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/serverless-fn:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          syft ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/serverless-fn:${{ github.sha }} -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json

      - name: Sign image with cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign --key cosign.key ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/serverless-fn:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Verify signature
        run: |
          cosign verify --key cosign.pub ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/serverless-fn:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Upload to Rekor
        run: |
          cosign upload blob -f attestation.json
```

## Failing Manifest (Unsigned Image)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: serverless-workload
spec:
  containers:
  - name: function
    image: registry.example.com/serverless-fn:abc123
```

## Passing Manifest (Signed Image)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: serverless-workload
spec:
  containers:
  - name: function
    image: registry.example.com/serverless-fn:signed-sha256
    imagePullPolicy: Always
```

## Local Verification

```bash
# Verify image signature
cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/serverless-fn:signed-sha256

# Verify attestation
cosign verify-attestation --type cyclonedx --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/serverless-fn:signed-sha256
```

## CI Verification Steps

1. Add Cosign verification step in CI pipeline
2. Block deployment if signature verification fails
3. Verify SBOM matches image contents
4. Check Rekor transparency log for attestation

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests end-to-end security design for multi-cloud Kubernetes workloads, focusing on identity, secret management, and policy enforcement with real-world tools.

## Key Concepts
- Zero-trust workload identity (SPIRE)
- Ephemeral credentials (Vault)
- Service mesh security (Istio, mTLS, AuthorizationPolicies)
- Policy-as-code (OPA/Rego)
- Egress controls to data lake and namespace isolation

## Sample Solution

### 1. SPIRE Workload Identity
```yaml
# spire-workload.yaml
apiVersion: spire.spiffe.io/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterSPIFFEID
metadata:
  name: data-platform-workload
spec:
  names:
    - data-service
    - analytics-service
    - etl-service
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      environment: production
```

### 2. Vault Integration for Secrets
```yaml
# vault-secret-store.yaml
apiVersion: secrets.hashicorp.com/v1beta1
kind: VaultSecret
metadata:
  name: data-lake-credentials
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  vaultAddress: https://vault.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:8200
  path: secret/data-lake
  provider: hcp
  refreshInterval: 1h
```

### 3. Istio AuthorizationPolicy
```yaml
# istio-authz.yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: data-lake-access
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: data-lake-gateway
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["spiffe://data-platform/data-service"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
        paths: ["/v1/tables/*"]
```

### 4. OPA Policy Example
```rego
#.rego
package kubernetes.admission

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  input.request.namespace == "restricted"
  not input.request.object.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  msg = "Pods must run as non-root"
}

allow[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Deployment"
  input.request.object.spec.template.spec.containers[_].securityContext.privileged
  msg = "Privileged containers not allowed"
}
```

### 5. CI Enforcement Check
```yaml
# .github/workflows/security-scan.yml
name: Security Scan
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  opa-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run OPA policy check
        run: |
          opa eval --fail-defined-deny \
            --data policy.rego \
            --input manifests/
```

## Key Takeaways
- SPIRE provides cryptographically secure workload identity
- Vault enables dynamic secret rotation without application changes
- Istio mTLS ensures service-to-service encryption
- OPA/Rego enforces admission control and runtime policies
